Satirical letter from Prozac about the 'quick fix' criticism; present-tense pharmacology, no forward-looking claims.
Short satire press release about Elon Musk; no forward-looking claims by the author.
Vicarious trauma among future MDMA-AT therapists; several practice-adoption predictions plus one own-organization pipeline claim (Acacia Clinics TMS for PTSD).

Written after the FDA complete response letter on MDMA-AT. Self-quote from an Aug 1 podcast and a call that the Lykos appeal is doomed. Phase 3 Camp / Burning Man section is pure joke and not logged. Lykos/Emerson statements are third-party and disputed, not logged.
Humorous chat with OpenAI about time dilation; one closing quip logged with sincere=false for recall only.

Psychopharmacology retraction of an MDMA-AT paper. One 'not approved anytime soon' call; one borderline present legal-exposure claim logged with forward_looking=false. Post text ends mid-sentence before the quoted federal law.
Fictional Mordor press release parodying a PTSD-drug company's reorganization after a failure (founder exit, ~75% workforce cut). No sincere forecast by the author.
Review of alcohol and bipolar disorder course. Advice ('should be advised not to drink') is normative with no predictive reading; not logged.

Part I on the 2024 final MHPAEA parity rule. Payer-behavior predictions plus one quoted UC Davis cost forecast (own_claim=false). Rule-mechanics descriptions (60-day DSM update, compliance checks) not logged.
tFUS introduction; title is the forecast. Author also lists claimed past wins (ERISA suits, accelerated TMS payment models, MDMA not approved, TMS better than meds) — retrospective, not logged.

statements.quote: It won’t get an FDA label, but it makes nightmares better.
statements.context: Closing line of a post on prazosin (Minipress), an old generic alpha-1 blocker approved for hypertension in 1988 and used off-label for PTSD nightmares. The author says it will never get an FDA label for PTSD because it is already generic and no sponsor will fund the trials.
statements.note: Implicit 'never' horizon; negative regulatory call about a generic drug.

statements.quote: Nobody's going to make any money if they get an FDA label—they are already generic.
statements.context: Setup for the prazosin discussion: older generic medications (prazosin among them) will not earn a sponsor money even if they get a new FDA label, so nobody pays for the trials. General economic claim about repurposing off-patent drugs.
statements.note: Borderline: general economic claim close to a truism; logged for recall.

statements.quote: To be clear, this problem only gets worse with time.
statements.context: The problem: off-patent chemicals never get developed into labeled treatments because no sponsor can profit ('drugs that can't make a bazillion dollars'). The author expects this problem to worsen over time.
statements.note: Vague trend claim; hard to resolve.

statements.quote: To put my dime down, I don't think MDMA-AT will be approved by the FDA when it meets to discuss the 10-1 and 9-2 against AdComm votes cautioning against approval of the combination product at this time.
statements.context: The author's headline call in the seventh 'Saving MDMA' article: the FDA will not approve Lykos Therapeutics' NDA for MDMA-assisted therapy at the pending decision, following the June 2024 AdComm votes of 10-1 and 9-2 against. Post dated 2024-06-26, before the FDA action date.
statements.confidence_phrase: I don't think MDMA-AT will be approved
statements.note: Explicit 'put my dime down' call; restates the stance of the earlier Saving MDMA series.

statements.quote: The most crucial reason this will happen? The FDA will find it expedient to inform the study sponsor that they don't have the safety data necessary to approve the drug.
statements.context: Predicted mechanism of the FDA's non-approval of MDMA-AT: the agency will tell Lykos it lacks the required safety data (EKG and laboratory work that Lykos was asked for and did not provide).
statements.note: Prediction of the stated grounds for the FDA decision, not just the outcome.

statements.quote: They can then kick the can down the road. They can buy time to finish their investigation into alleged misconduct in the trials.
statements.context: Continuation of the predicted FDA mechanism on MDMA-AT: by requesting more safety data, the FDA can delay the decision and gain time to complete its investigation into alleged misconduct in the Lykos/MAPS trials.
statements.note: Hedged with 'can'; describes expected FDA delay tactic.

statements.quote: But you're not guaranteed that approval at that first meeting. Sometimes, it's gonna take years.
statements.context: Lesson drawn from the flibanserin (Addyi) history (NDA 2009, denials, approval with REMS in 2015) and applied to MDMA-AT: approval is not guaranteed at the first decision and can take years.
statements.note: Borderline: general statement about FDA process, applied to MDMA-AT by context.

statements.quote: Either be prepared to spend much, much much more, because that's on average what it costs, or it may be that you don't have the access to capital necessary to bring a new therapeutic to market in the United States?
statements.context: After citing a 2020 study putting the median cost of bringing a new drug to market at $1.3b and noting Lykos has spent only a tiny fraction: Lykos will need to spend far more, or may lack the capital to bring MDMA-AT to market.
statements.note: Addressed to Lykos in the second person; compound either/or claim about capital needs.

statements.quote: Can MDMA get over the line? Based on the experience of Flibanserin, of course.
statements.context: Closing of the post: the author expects MDMA can eventually be approved, by analogy to flibanserin (Addyi), which was approved in 2015 after multiple denials, provided the sponsor puts in the time and money. He adds doubts about whether it is worth it financially.
statements.note: Eventual-approval call; sits alongside the near-term non-approval call in the same post.

statements.quote: A new Apex predator is in town. It doesn't care if you're in the water. And it sure as F- isn’t going to disclose it.
statements.context: Closing of a satirical piece in which Optum/UnitedHealthcare 'acquires' the largest great white shark nursery off Rockaway Beach. The sincere underlying claim: UnitedHealth Group will keep making acquisitions without public disclosure because they fall below the 'material to earnings' threshold.
statements.note: Satirical framing; the non-disclosure claim reads as a real expectation.

statements.quote: Individuals trained in psychedelic-assisted therapy are not likely a dime dozen. It's going to be expensive to get that training.
statements.context: Written while the FDA decision on Lykos's MDMA-AT NDA was pending. The author argues the modality will require trained specialists, who will be scarce, and that the training will be expensive.
statements.note: Second sentence carries 'It's going to be expensive'.

statements.quote: Psychedelic-assisted therapists, both for the economic reality of their lives and for the needs of patients, are going to be expected to do a lot of psychedelic-assisted therapy. This means they're going to be encountering humans who suffered tremendous trauma.
statements.context: If MDMA-AT reaches practice, its therapists will be expected to do high volumes of psychedelic-assisted therapy and thus face heavy exposure to patients' trauma narratives; the setup for the vicarious-trauma argument.
statements.note: Compound claim about future therapist workload and exposure.

statements.quote: We have heard we will need many more therapists, including under-represented populations.
statements.context: Restatement of the MDMA-AT field's stated need for many more therapists, including from under-represented populations; the author adopts it as the premise for his argument that MDMA-AT will traumatize more therapists.
statements.note: Restatement of others' claim ('We have heard'); author builds on it, so own_claim kept true.

statements.quote: A successful drive to recruit more under-represented people means more trauma for those new therapists, too.
statements.context: Conditional: if the MDMA-AT field succeeds in recruiting more under-represented therapists, those new therapists will be exposed to more vicarious trauma. Preceded by the claim that MDMA-AT traumatizes twice as many people per patient treated.
statements.note: Conditional claim.

statements.quote: It’s also entirely predictable to estimate that only more severe trauma cases will get this novel therpay.
statements.context: Prediction about who will receive MDMA-AT if it reaches practice: only the more severe PTSD cases. 'therpay' is the author's typo for therapy.
statements.note: Quote keeps the author's typo 'therpay'.

statements.quote: Thus, the vicarious trauma among MDMA-AT therapists might be expected to be worse and more toxic for the cohort of MDMA-AT practitioners given higher-grade PTSD in those patients.
statements.context: Conclusion of the argument: because MDMA-AT patients will have more severe PTSD, vicarious trauma among MDMA-AT therapists will be worse than for other trauma therapists.
statements.note: Hedged clinical-workforce prediction.

statements.quote: We even have an fMRI-Guided Accelerated TMS therapy5 in the pipeline for the treatment of PTSD, co-developed by colleagues at Acacia Clinics and Harvard.
statements.context: List of non-talk trauma treatments the author's organizations offer or develop (PRISM neurofeedback at Fermata, Nightware, magnesium-ibogaine). Here an fMRI-guided accelerated TMS therapy for PTSD, co-developed at Acacia Clinics (the author's clinic) and Harvard, is 'in the pipeline'. The '5' is a footnote marker to Siddiqi et al. 2024.
statements.note: Own organization (Acacia Clinics): coder may mark CONTROL. Weak pipeline claim.

statements.quote: If they just rubber stamp things and someone dies, or something awful happens, someone is going to come back and make a documentary on Netflix like they did about Perdue Pharma and highlight the FDA official who signed off on the thing after some dubious party.
statements.context: The author quotes his own August 1, 2024 statement on the Psychiatry Tomorrow Podcast, made before the FDA's complete response letter on MDMA-AT, as a call he got right ('I knew it'): a conditional about FDA reviewers' incentive not to rubber-stamp approvals.
statements.note: Self-quote from a podcast dated Aug 1, reproduced Aug 10 after the CRL; hypothetical conditional. 'Perdue' is the author's spelling.

statements.quote: So, an appeal makes sense…no matter how doomed to failure.
statements.context: After the FDA's complete response letter asking Lykos for an additional Phase 3 trial of midomafetamine (MDMA-AT), Lykos said it would request a meeting to seek reconsideration. The author cites CDER appeal statistics (16% granted, 2003-2014) and expects the Lykos appeal to fail.
statements.note: Prediction that the Lykos request for reconsideration will not succeed.

statements.quote: This is also, I fear, the way the world ends —with slacker math and narcissism.
statements.context: Closing quip of a humorous post about arguing with an OpenAI model over a special-relativity calculation for daylight saving time, and about an AI-generated flattering picture of the author. Hyperbolic joke about AI, not a real expectation.
statements.note: Joke; logged for recall only.

statements.quote: The course of the last several weeks has proven that, although this won't be an approved therapeutic anytime soon, it continues to be one hell of a story.
statements.context: Written the day after the FDA requested an additional trial for Lykos's MDMA-AT NDA and as the journal Psychopharmacology retracted an MDMA-AT paper for undisclosed protocol violations at the MP4 site: the author says MDMA-AT will not be approved anytime soon.
statements.note: Post-CRL restatement of the non-approval call with a 'not soon' horizon.

statements.quote: Yes, dear readers, but it’s also possibly a crime.
statements.context: The author argues the retracted MDMA-AT paper, whose authors confirmed they knew of MP4-site protocol violations at submission and did not disclose them, is evidence of a potential criminal matter under federal law on fraudulent data submitted to the FDA. A present legal-exposure claim about MAPS/MAPS PBC authors with only an implicit possibility of future proceedings.
statements.note: Borderline: asserts present legal status, not a prediction of prosecution; logged for recall.

statements.quote: The inclusion of these will, I suspect, be crucial and at the expense of excellent treatment for the rest of the mental health conditions.
statements.context: Part I on the 2024 final MHPAEA parity rule from the Department of Labor and HHS, which defines MH/SUD conditions by the current ICD or DSM and so includes dementia and autism. The author expects coverage of these two expensive diagnoses to come at the expense of treatment quality for other mental health conditions.
statements.note: 'These' refers to dementia and autism.

statements.quote: Their forecasts for ASD-related medical, nonmedical and productivity losses are $268 billion for 2015 and $461 billion for 2025. The researchers noted that these estimates are conservative and, if ASD prevalence continues to increase as it has in recent years, the costs could reach $1 trillion by 2025.
statements.context: Quoted UC Davis research summary the author cites to show why classifying autism (ASD) as a mental health condition under the parity rule is 'a huge deal, financially'. Third-party forecast of US autism-related costs.
statements.note: Quoted third-party (UC Davis) forecast; author cites it as support and does not restate it in his own words.

statements.quote: One could also imagine a world where you made general medical and surgical care more awful to bring both into parity. It’s not outside of our imagination that payers could do that, too.
statements.context: On how payers might meet the parity rule's comparison metrics (is MH/SUD paid for and accessible like medical/surgical care): rather than improving MH/SUD coverage, payers could worsen medical/surgical coverage to reach parity.
statements.note: Hedged possibility about payer behavior.

statements.quote: Another strategy to make MH/SUD parity happen? Just make it cost more! If you spend as much on MH/SUD care as you do on neurosurgery, the total cost of care goes up, and the parity check works out ok.
statements.context: Second hypothesized payer response to the parity rule: raise MH/SUD spending so the parity check passes while total cost of care rises. The author frames payer incentives as optimizing profit and medical loss ratio rather than saving money.
statements.note: Borderline: hypothetical strategy stated as a possibility, no explicit confidence word.

statements.quote: One expensive-enough drug or procedure for autism, Alzheimer’s, or any condition really could swing the balance in some plans.
statements.context: Closing of the parity post: a single costly autism or Alzheimer's drug or procedure could tip some health plans' parity math, followed by 'Be careful what you wish for.'
statements.note: Hedged; vague resolution criteria.

statements.quote: Transcranial Focused Ultrasound (tFUS) is Coming to Brain Health
statements.context: Title and thesis of the post: the author predicts low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound will become a brain-health (psychiatric) treatment, able to reach deep brain targets TMS cannot. He notes Acacia Clinics (his clinic) is running a tFUS anxiety trial and names Samn.ai, OpenWater and BrainSonix as companies in the race, with over $100m raised at OpenWater.
statements.note: Title-level call; author's own clinic runs a tFUS trial (possible CONTROL interest).
